claims.text: Dealloying-based synthesis can produce three-dimensional nanoframeworks of noble metal–based high-entropy alloys.
Dealloying selectively dissolves less noble elements from a precursor alloy.
Selective dissolution induces self-organization into a porous, interconnected structure.
The proposed precursor is a homogeneous NM-HEA containing both noble and less noble metallic elements.
Controlled acidic etching can selectively remove less noble metals from the precursor.
Controlling pH, temperature, and etching duration can enable selective dissolution without structural collapse.
Selective removal of alloy constituents forms nanoscale porosity.
Selective removal of alloy constituents forms an interconnected framework.
Dissolution of less noble metals causes the remaining atoms to rearrange.
The atomic rearrangement produces a thermodynamically favorable, interconnected three-dimensional porous network.
The interconnected porous network increases the catalyst's active surface area.
The interconnected porous network increases structural complexity.
Dealloying transforms the NM-HEA into a three-dimensional nanoframework.
The resulting nanoframework has enhanced catalytic activity because of its high surface area and atomic-level diversity.
The non-dealloyed NM-HEA precursor has a uniform, dense structure.
The method is primarily effective when alloy components differ sufficiently in nobility to permit selective etching.
Dealloying may be less effective when the compositional or nobility contrast among components is low.
